_doc: Item bank v2. Each question has 6 behavioural anchors ordered by sophistication. levelMap[i] is the level anchor i demonstrates (0=Pre-Pilot 1=Pilot 2=Builder 3=Multiplier). The anchor IS the measurement -- no averaging of agreement. Window is the last two weeks throughout (Fabia). Craft skills, not AI volume: a heavy AI user without the craft scores Pre-Pilot, which is the point.
_naming: Say "Claude" when the question is about interacting with the model directly (asking it something, judging what it gave back). Say "AI" when it is about the broader category -- builds, automations, agents. Every stem must name one or the other, so no question can be answered about non-AI work.
_writingRules: Every stem is a complete question ending in 'what was most true?'. Every anchor is a complete first-person sentence that reads on its own -- no sentence-completion fragments. Anchors describe what happened, never what you are.

reach._howToAnswer: Think of a specific time in the last two weeks when you brought AI to something unfamiliar, or had to work to get a useful answer out of it. Pick the option closest to what you actually did — not what you would do on a good day.

questions.stem: Think of a task in the last two weeks that you hadn't tried with AI before. What was most true?
anchors: I stayed with the kinds of tasks I already knew it could handle.
I tried it, and when the first answer was poor I moved on.
I rephrased and tried a few different angles until it worked.
I worked out what I was actually asking for before I asked.
I noticed the kinds of problems it keeps failing at, and stopped bringing it those.
I changed what I thought was worth attempting at all, because of what it turned out to be good at.

questions.stem: Think of something you needed from Claude in the last two weeks that really mattered. What was most true about how you asked for it?
anchors: I described the task and took what came back.
I gave it some background about the task.
I gave it the background, who it was for, and what a good answer would look like.
I told it what I did not want, as well as what I did.
I realised my first question was the wrong question, and reframed it before going on.
I set the context up once, so that I — or someone else — wouldn't have to explain it again next time.

questions.stem: AI capabilities keep changing. In the last two weeks, what was most true for you?
anchors: I hadn't really noticed anything change.
I heard about new things it could do, but I haven't tried them.
I tried something I'd heard was newly possible.
I went looking for what had changed since I last checked.
I changed a way of working I already had, because something better became possible.
I changed what my team attempts at all, based on what became possible.

autonomy._howToAnswer: Think about recurring work you actually changed with AI in the last two weeks — a process, a handoff, something you do every week. These questions are about the thinking you did before and around the change, not how much AI you used.

questions.skill: Persistence — does anything outlive the conversation
questions.stem: Think about the work you did with AI in the last two weeks. What was most true about what came out of it?
anchors: Nothing I made outlives the conversation it happened in.
I've saved a few prompts that I reuse.
I have a setup I go back to that works the same way each time.
I have something running that I would have to rebuild if I lost it.
Someone else uses something I built, without asking me how.
A whole part of my function works differently because of something I built.

questions.stem: Think of a piece of recurring work you tried to speed up or automate with AI in the last two weeks. What was most true about what you did first?
anchors: I didn't change any recurring work.
I asked Claude to do the task faster.
I thought about which part of it was actually slow.
I wrote out how the work really runs today, step by step, before changing anything.
I mapped it, found the step that was the real bottleneck, and changed only that.
I redesigned the work around what's now possible, instead of speeding up its existing shape.

questions.stem: Think of a time in the last two weeks when you changed a step in a process because of something you built or automated with AI. What was most true about how far you looked?
anchors: I changed my own step, and that was the scope of it.
I let people know afterwards.
I checked what happened to the step immediately after mine.
I traced what my change would do further downstream before I made it.
I found something my change would break for someone else, and designed around it.
I looked at the whole flow and moved where the work happens, not just how fast it happens.

navigation._howToAnswer: These are about judgment — deciding whether to trust an output, whether to use AI at all, and which approach fits. There is no penalty for the lower options. Answer for what you actually did in the last two weeks.

questions._note: Anchors are Fabia's own wording, near-verbatim.
questions.stem: Think of something Claude gave you in the last two weeks that you were going to act on. What was most true about how you checked it?
anchors: I trusted it without revision.
I looked for mistakes, but I didn't spend significant time on it.
I made sure the fidelity against the source was there before I shipped it.
I stopped and pivoted as soon as I saw a deviation that changed the meaning of what I was trying to achieve.
I built the check into the process, so it gets caught without me.
I spent time upfront defining the guardrails, so the output represents the goals of my build and the needs of the business.

questions.skill: Restraint — knowing when not to use AI
questions.stem: In the last two weeks, when you were deciding whether to use AI for something, what was most true?
anchors: If AI could plausibly do it, I used AI.
I used AI unless it obviously wouldn't work.
I thought about whether it was a good fit first.
At least once I decided AI was the wrong tool, and did something simpler instead.
I can say which kinds of work in my role AI should not touch, and why.
I've talked my team out of an AI solution that wasn't the right answer.

questions.skill: Choosing the approach — rule, automation, or agent
questions.stem: Think of something in the last two weeks you wanted AI to handle repeatedly, without you running it each time. What was most true about how you set it up?
anchors: I didn't have anything like that.
I redid it by hand each time, with AI's help.
I saved something reusable, and ran it myself when I needed it.
I chose deliberately between a simple rule, an automation, and something agentic.
I can explain why I picked the approach I picked, and what would make me pick differently.
I've set which of these my team reaches for, and when.

generalization._howToAnswer: These are about the people and teams around your AI work — whether what you figured out travels, and what your changes do to everyone else. Think of a specific thing you built or changed with AI in the last two weeks, and who it touched.

questions.stem: Think of a way of using AI that you figured out in one part of your job in the last two weeks. What was most true about where it ended up?
anchors: It stayed where it was.
I mentioned it to someone.
I used it again somewhere else myself.
I adapted it for a different situation, and it worked there too.
Someone on another team now uses it.
It became how a whole function does that kind of work.

questions._note: Fabia: what happens when your team adopts and the teams around it don't.
questions.stem: Think of a time in the last two weeks when your way of working changed because of something you built with AI. What was most true about the people it affected?
anchors: I didn't think about the effect on anyone else.
I told the people who were directly affected.
I checked whether the people who hand work to me could keep up.
I found a place where my change left another team out of step, and I flagged it.
I designed the handoff so the other team didn't have to change anything to work with me.
I got the connected parts of the system brought up to speed too, not just my own.

questions.stem: Think of something you built with AI in the last two weeks that someone else might use. What was most true about how you built it?
anchors: I built it for me.
I'd explain it to someone if they asked.
I wrote down how to use it.
I built it so someone with less context than me could run it without asking me.
I watched someone else use it, and fixed what confused them.
I've set what "usable by someone else" has to mean on my team.

execution._howToAnswer: These are about quality and care — how you know AI output is good, what you let into shared docs and systems, and what happens to your AI builds over time. Think of something specific you shipped or maintained with AI in the last two weeks.

questions.stem: Think of something you shipped with AI's help in the last two weeks. What was most true about how you judged whether it was good?
anchors: I went by whether it looked right.
I read it over before sending it.
I had a clear idea of what good meant for that work before I started.
I checked it against that standard, not just against my instinct.
I have a repeatable way of checking quality that doesn't depend on my mood that day.
I've defined what good looks like for the work my team ships with AI.

questions.stem: Think of AI output that went into something lasting in the last two weeks — a shared doc, a dataset, a system. What was most true?
anchors: I hadn't thought about it in those terms.
I fixed the obvious errors before it went in.
I cut the filler and padding that AI tends to add.
I made sure it added something a reader couldn't get elsewhere, rather than just adding volume.
I have a rule for what's allowed into shared docs and data, and I hold to it.
I've raised the standard for what my team lets AI put into shared systems.

questions.stem: Think of something you've built with AI that other people now rely on. What was most true in the last two weeks?
anchors: I don't have anything that others rely on.
It works for now, and I'd deal with problems when they come.
I know what would break it, and I keep an eye on that.
I've thought about who is affected if it's wrong, not just whether it's convenient.
It has an owner, a way to check it's still right, and a way to turn it off.
I've set how long these things are meant to last, and who is accountable when they don't.
